Clinical risk distribution is a critical area of study in cardiovascular medicine, particularly when evaluating the real-world outcomes of risk stratification tools like the [[CHA2DS2-VASc]] score. This score is widely used to estimate the risk of stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation and to guide anticoagulant therapy. However, analyzing the distribution of these scores among patients who experience severe adverse events, such as an [[Intrakraniel blødning]] (intracranial bleeding), provides essential context regarding the safety and predictive limitations of these models.

In [[Danmark]], national registry data has highlighted that a substantial proportion of severe bleeding events occur in patients who are traditionally classified as having a low thromboembolic risk. Among prevalent atrial fibrillation patients who suffered an intracranial bleed in Denmark, 36.7% had a CHA2DS2-VASc score of exactly 1 [^src1]. Broadening this scope, recent data indicates that 41.1% of all intracranial bleeding events occurred among patients with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of either 0 or 1 [^src2]. 

These findings underscore a significant clinical paradox: while low CHA2DS2-VASc scores correctly identify patients at lower risk for ischemic stroke, a large absolute number of severe bleeding complications still arise within this "low-risk" cohort. This distribution challenges clinicians to carefully weigh the risks and benefits of antithrombotic therapies, as the occurrence of intracranial bleeding is not strictly confined to high-risk populations.

## Claims

**AFDK_2023.pdf, page 98**
- Blandt prævalente atrieflimren-patienter med intrakraniel blødning i Danmark havde 36,7 % en CHA2DS2-VASc-score på 1 [^src1] (cha2ds2-vasc, intrakraniel-bloedning, danmark)

**AFDK_2024.pdf, page 54**
- 41,1% af intrakranielle blødninger optrådte blandt patienter med en CHA2DS2-VASc score på 0 eller 1 [^src1] (cha2ds2-vasc, intrakraniel-bloedning)
